etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Inherited from Middle English halle, from Old English heall (“hall, dwelling, house; palace, temple; law-court”), from Proto-West Germanic *hallu, from Proto-Germanic *hallō (“hall”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, conceal”).

Cognate with Scots hall, haw (“hall”), Dutch hal (“hall”), German Halle (“hall”), Norwegian hall (“hall”), Swedish hall (“hall”), Icelandic höll (“palace”), Latin cella (“room, cell”), Sanskrit शाला (śā́lā, “house, mansion, hall”). Doublet of cell and cella.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter XIII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: We tiptoed into the house, up the stairs and along the hall into the room where the Professor had been spending so much of his time.

definitions.definition: A manor house (originally because a magistrate's court was held in the hall of his mansion).

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Taming of the Shrew”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: But Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendome, Kate of Kate-hall.

definitions.definition: A building providing student accommodation at a university.
The principal room of a secular medieval building.
(obsolete) Cleared passageway through a crowd, as for dancing.

quote.citation: 1633 (first performance), Ben Jonson, “A Tale of a Tub. A Comedy […]”, in The Works of Beniamin Jonson, […] (Third Folio), London:  […]  Thomas Hodgkin, for H[enry] Herringman, E. Brewster, T. Bassett, R[ichard] Chiswell, M. Wotton, G. Conyers, published 1692, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Then cry, a hall, a hall! Come, father Rosin, with your fiddle now.

definitions.definition: A place for special professional education, or for conferring professional degrees or licences.
(Oxbridge) A college's canteen, which is often but not always coterminous with a traditional hall.
(Oxbridge slang) A meal served and eaten at a college's hall.
